Line 87: 7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
Line 89: 8\. **Record retention of six (6) years** per 45 CFR § 164.530(j), covering all HIPAA-required documentation including the BAA itself, policies and procedures, training records, and incident records; and
Line 91: 9\. **Return or destruction of PHI at termination**, with exceptions where return or destruction is infeasible, in which case the protections of the BAA must extend to all retained PHI for as long as it is maintained.
Line 93: Negotiators should be particularly alert to vendor DPA templates that reference GDPR Article 28 processor requirements but omit any reference to HIPAA. Where a vendor will process PHI, the absence of a BAA renders the DPA non-compliant regardless of how robust the GDPR provisions may be.
Line 95: **[2.2 CCPA / CPRA]{.underline}**
Line 97: Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient-facing platform, provider network, and marketing and analytics activities. This volume substantially exceeds the CCPA/CPRA applicability thresholds and places Pinnacle squarely within the statute\'s scope as a \"**Business**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d).
Line 99: Vendors that process California personal information on Pinnacle\'s behalf must qualify as \"**Service Providers**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag). The Service Provider designation is not automatic; it requires specific contractual provisions that restrict the vendor\'s use, retention, and disclosure of personal information received from Pinnacle. Without these contractual provisions, a vendor may be deemed a \"third party\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which could expose Pinnacle to claims that it has \"sold\" or \"shared\" personal information in violation of the statute.
Line 105: > • A **prohibition on combining** personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information received from any other person or entity, or collected from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA;
Line 111: These provisions are mandatory for all vendors with access to California resident data. A vendor DPA that omits these provisions, or that contains language inconsistent with the Service Provider classification, must be redlined before execution. Detailed negotiation positions for CCPA/CPRA terms are set forth in Section 7 of this playbook.
Line 113: **[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**
Line 117: Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
Line 119: > • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;
Line 125: GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.
Line 127: **[Section 3: Definitions --- Required Contractual Definitions]{.underline}**
Line 131: **[3.1 Required Defined Terms by Regulatory Regime]{.underline}**
Line 169: **CCPA/CPRA Definitions (per Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140)**
Line 171: The following terms must be defined consistently with the CCPA/CPRA statutory definitions:
Line 187: **[3.2 Negotiation Positions for Definitions]{.underline}**
Line 189: **Must-have:** The DPA must include all three sets of definitions where the vendor processes data subject to multiple regulatory regimes. Many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted to address GDPR only and will include GDPR definitions but omit HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA definitions entirely. Where this is the case, the negotiator must require the addition of both the HIPAA definitions and the CCPA/CPRA definitions before the DPA is finalized. A DPA that covers PHI but lacks the defined term \"Protected Health Information\" creates ambiguity regarding the scope of the vendor\'s obligations and may be insufficient to satisfy the BAA requirements of 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Similarly, a DPA that covers California personal information but lacks the defined terms \"Service Provider,\" \"Sale,\" and \"Share\" may fail to establish the vendor\'s qualification as a Service Provider under the CCPA/CPRA, with potentially significant regulatory consequences for Pinnacle.
Line 191: **Nice-to-have:** A single, integrated definitions section within the DPA body, rather than separate definitions scattered across the DPA, BAA exhibit, and CCPA addendum. An integrated definitions section reduces the risk of inconsistent or conflicting definitions and simplifies interpretation and enforcement.
Line 193: **Fallback:** HIPAA definitions may be incorporated by reference to the BAA exhibit, and CCPA/CPRA definitions may be incorporated by reference to a CCPA/CPRA Addendum, so long as both the BAA exhibit and the CCPA/CPRA Addendum are appended to and expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should confirm that the cross-references are accurate and that the defined terms in the exhibit or addendum are consistent with the terms used in the DPA body.
Line 195: **[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**
Line 197: This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.
Line 199: ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
Line 201: **[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**
Line 203: **Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
Line 205: The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:
Line 207: > **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.
Line 209: > **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.
Line 219: > \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
Line 221: > **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
Line 223: > **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.
Line 225: > **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.
Line 227: > **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.
Line 229: **Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.
Line 231: **Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
Line 233: **[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**
Line 235: Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.
Line 237: If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.
Line 239: For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.
Line 241: Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.
Line 243: **[Section 5: Breach Notification]{.underline}**
Line 245: Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.
Line 249: **[5.1 Notification Timeline]{.underline}**
Line 251: **Must-have:** Vendor must notify Pinnacle of any actual or reasonably suspected breach of Personal Data, PHI, or California Personal Information within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. For purposes of this requirement, \"**discovery**\" means the first day on which the breach is known to the vendor, or the first day on which the breach, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the vendor. This definition is consistent with the HITECH Act\'s definition of discovery at 42 U.S.C. § 17382.
Line 257: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides **preliminary telephonic notification** within **four (4) hours** of discovery, followed by **written notification** within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. The telephonic notification should include the vendor\'s initial assessment of the nature of the incident, the categories of data potentially affected, and the vendor\'s immediate containment measures. This telephonic-plus-written approach allows Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team to begin its assessment in parallel with the vendor\'s investigation.
Line 259: **Fallback:** The 24-hour notification timeline is a **firm requirement**. Pinnacle will not accept timelines exceeding 24 hours for processor-to-controller notification. Negotiators should be aware that many vendor DPA templates propose **48-hour** or **72-hour** notification timelines. These proposals must be rejected and redlined to 24 hours. The following talking points may be useful in negotiations:
Line 263: > • A **48-hour** processor-to-controller timeline is insufficient because it compresses Pinnacle\'s time to assess the breach, engage legal counsel, activate its incident response plan, and prepare its own regulatory notifications. Under HIPAA, Pinnacle must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, and discovery is deemed to occur when the Business Associate notifies the Covered Entity. Under CCPA/CPRA, California\'s data breach notification statute (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82) requires notification \"in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.\" Every hour of delay in vendor notification reduces Pinnacle\'s available response window.
Line 267: **[5.2 HIPAA-Specific Breach Notification Obligations]{.underline}**
Line 269: **Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must include the full HIPAA/HITECH breach notification cascade, reflecting the following obligations:
Line 283: The DPA/BAA must clearly allocate responsibility for each step of this notification cascade. While vendor (as Business Associate) is responsible for the initial notification to Pinnacle, Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) is responsible for notifications to individuals, HHS, and the media. However, vendor must provide Pinnacle with all information reasonably necessary to enable Pinnacle to fulfill its notification obligations.
Line 285: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s breach notification to Pinnacle must include, at a minimum, the following information:
Line 299: **Must-have --- Late Notification Penalties:** Breach notification timelines are only meaningful if vendor faces commercial consequences for failure to comply. Pinnacle\'s preferred penalty clause is as follows:
Line 303: > **Fallback:** If the vendor proposes a counter to the liquidated damages provision, Pinnacle will accept a per-day penalty with a reasonable cap, provided that the per-day amount is **no lower than \$2,500** and the cap is **no lower than \$250,000**. Any vendor proposal below these thresholds must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park.
Line 305: **[5.3 Breach Notification Content Requirements]{.underline}**
Line 325: **[Section 6: Liability and Indemnification]{.underline}**
Line 327: Liability provisions are among the most heavily negotiated terms in any DPA. The allocation of financial risk between Pinnacle and its vendors must reflect the magnitude of the data at stake, the severity of potential regulatory penalties, and the operational and reputational harm that a data breach or compliance failure could cause. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required liability framework, including liability caps, carve-outs, and indemnification obligations.
Line 329: Pinnacle\'s position on liability is informed by the following considerations: (i) a breach of PHI affecting Pinnacle\'s approximately 2.1 million US patients could result in HIPAA penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year, plus class action litigation exposure; (ii) a CCPA/CPRA violation could result in statutory damages of \$100 to \$750 per consumer per incident, which at 890,000 California residents represents potential exposure of \$89 million to \$667.5 million; and (iii) GDPR penalties can reach up to €20 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Against this backdrop, vendor liability caps that are a fraction of annual fees are commercially unreasonable and legally inadequate.
Line 331: **[6.1 Liability Cap]{.underline}**
Line 333: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under the DPA must be no less than **two times (2x) the total annual fees** attributable to the affected data processing activity.
Line 349: **Must-have:** Liability must be **uncapped** for the following categories of claims:
Line 351: > \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
Line 353: > \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
Line 357: > \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.
Line 359: **Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.
Line 361: **Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).
Line 363: **Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.
Line 365: **Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.
Line 367: **[6.2 Indemnification]{.underline}**
Line 369: **Must-have:** Vendor must indemnify, des different governing law depending on the nature of the claim and the data involved:
Line 515: > **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.
Line 519: **Nice-to-have:** Delaware law for all matters, including EU data disputes. However, this position is unlikely to be accepted by EU-based vendors and may conflict with GDPR mandatory provisions that require application of EU Member State law for certain data protection matters, including enforcement actions by supervisory authorities.
Line 521: **Fallback:** German law for EU data disputes is acceptable, provided that Delaware law for US data disputes is preserved as a must-have. The bifurcation itself --- applying US law to US data disputes and EU law to EU data disputes --- is the critical structural requirement. Pinnacle will not accept a DPA that applies a single non-US governing law (e.g., German law) to disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information.
Line 523: **[10.2 Dispute Resolution Forum]{.underline}**
Line 525: **Must-have:** The DPA must include the following forum selection provisions:
Line 537: **Nice-to-have:** Federal court jurisdiction (Western District of Texas) for all disputes, including EU data disputes. This is unlikely to be accepted by EU vendors but should be proposed as the opening position.
Line 539: **Fallback:** Pinnacle will accept arbitration for EU data disputes but will **NOT** accept non-US arbitration or non-US courts for disputes involving US data (PHI, CCPA-covered data, or any other US personal information). Any vendor DPA that applies a non-US governing law and/or a non-US dispute resolution forum to US data disputes must be **redlined**. Escalate to Margaret Yuen-Park and Rachel Osterfeld (Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP) if the vendor insists on a non-US forum for US data disputes.
Line 541: **Note for negotiators:** Some vendor templates apply a single governing law (e.g., German law) and a single arbitration forum (e.g., Munich) to all disputes under the DPA, regardless of the type of data or the jurisdiction of the affected data subjects. This approach is problematic for several reasons:
Line 545: > • CCPA/CPRA enforcement is under **California jurisdiction** (California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency). A German arbitration clause may create uncertainty regarding the enforceability of CCPA-related contractual provisions.
Line 551: **[Section 11: International Data Transfers]{.underline}**
Line 553: While this playbook focuses primarily on US requirements, cross-border data transfers directly affect US data and must be addressed in vendor DPA negotiations. For example, EU data may be transferred to the US for disaster recovery or support purposes, and US data may be accessed remotely by vendor personnel located in the EU or other jurisdictions. The DPA must establish clear transfer mechanisms and documentation requirements for all such scenarios.
Line 555: **[11.1 Transfer Mechanisms]{.underline}**
Line 557: **Must-have:** Where vendor or any subprocessor transfers personal data from the EU/EEA to a third country (including the United States), the DPA must specify the applicable lawful transfer mechanism for each transfer scenario. Acceptable transfer mechanisms include:
Line 559: > **(a) EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021. The appropriate module must be selected for each transfer relationship:
Line 561: > • **Module 2** (Controller-to-Processor): For transfers from Pinnacle EU B.V. (as Controller) to a vendor (as Processor) located outside the EEA;
Line 563: > • **Module 3** (Processor-to-Subprocessor): For transfers from a vendor (as Processor) to a subprocessor located outside the EEA; and
Line 565: > • **Module 4** (Processor-to-Controller): Where applicable, for reverse transfers.
Line 567: > **(b) EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\")** certification: Acceptable only if the receiving entity (vendor or subprocessor) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities. Negotiators should verify the vendor\'s DPF certification status on the International Trade Administration\'s Data Privacy Framework List (dataprivacyframework.gov) before relying on this mechanism.
Line 571: **Must-have:** The DPA must address **all** transfer scenarios, including:
Line 573: > • Primary data hosting and processing transfers (e.g., data stored in an EEA data center and processed by a US-based vendor);
Line 575: > • Disaster recovery and business continuity transfers (e.g., data replicated to a US-based backup facility);
Line 579: > • Subprocessor transfers (e.g., vendor engages a subprocessor in a third country to perform specific processing activities).
Line 581: **Must-have:** Vendor must conduct and document a **Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\")** for each transfer of personal data to a third country. The TIA must assess the laws and practices of the recipient country that may affect the protection of the transferred data, including government surveillance laws, and must be made available to Pinnacle upon request. Where the TIA identifies risks that cannot be mitigated by supplementary measures, the transfer mechanism may need to be reconsidered.
Line 583: **Must-have:** If a subprocessor is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs must be executed with the appropriate module (typically Module 3, Processor-to-Subprocessor) before any personal data is transferred to that subprocessor.
Line 585: **Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle pre-approves the specific SCC modules for each transfer relationship during DPA negotiation, ensuring clarity and reducing the need for post-execution amendments as transfer relationships evolve.
Line 587: **Fallback:** If vendor\'s DPA template attaches only one SCC module (which is common), Pinnacle will require the addition of all applicable modules before execution. The negotiator should assess the vendor\'s transfer relationships and subprocessor arrangements to determine which modules are required and ensure that they are included in the DPA as executed.
Line 589: **[Section 12: Subprocessing Requirements]{.underline}**
Line 591: Vendors frequently engage subprocessors to perform specific data processing activities on their behalf. Because Pinnacle\'s data may ultimately be processed by entities with which Pinnacle has no direct contractual relationship, the DPA must include robust subprocessor requirements that ensure end-to-end protection. This Section works in conjunction with Section 8 (Audit Rights --- subprocessor coverage) and Section 4 (HIPAA BAA --- subcontractor flow-down).
Line 593: **[12.1 Subprocessor Obligations]{.underline}**
Line 595: **Must-have:** Vendor must impose on each subprocessor **substantially the same** data protection obligations as those imposed on vendor under the DPA. This flow-down requirement applies to all applicable regulatory regimes, including:
Line 597: > • **HIPAA BAA flow-down terms**: Each subprocessor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI must be bound by BAA obligations equivalent to those in vendor\'s BAA with Pinnacle (per 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
Line 599: > • **CCPA/CPRA Service Provider restrictions**: Each subprocessor that processes California personal information must be contractually restricted from selling, sharing, combining, or using the personal information for purposes other than those specified in the agreement;
Line 601: > • **GDPR Article 28 requirements**: Each subprocessor must be bound by a written contract that provides the same level of data protection as the vendor\'s DPA with Pinnacle (per GDPR Art. 28(4)); and
Line 603: > • **Confidentiality obligations**: Each subprocessor must be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the DPA.
Line 605: **Must-have:** Vendor remains **fully liable** for the acts and omissions of its subprocessors. **[Section 1: Purpose and Scope of This Playbook]{.underline}**

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents**, triggering obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"). Given the significant volume of California resident data processed by Pinnacle and its vendors, CCPA/CPRA compliance is a primary concern in all vendor DPA negotiations involving consumer-facing data.
> • **HIPAA/HITECH**, including Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") requirements;
> • **CCPA/CPRA**, including Service Provider qualification and certification requirements;
> • **GDPR**, including Article 28 processor requirements and cross-border data transfer mechanisms; and

**Important Note:** This playbook does NOT replace the requirement for outside counsel review of DPAs involving novel or high-risk processing activities. Negotiators must escalate to **Rachel Osterfeld** at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP for matters involving cross-border transfers to jurisdictions without adequacy decisions, novel HIPAA scenarios (including first-of-kind technology deployments involving PHI), regulatory enforcement actions or investigations, or any matter where the vendor\'s proposed terms deviate materially from the positions set forth herein and the applicable fallback position is inadequate to protect Pinnacle\'s interests.
**[Section 2: Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**

The three regimes are: (1) the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009 (\"**HIPAA/HITECH**\"); (2) the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"); and (3) the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (\"**GDPR**\"). Each regime imposes its own definitions, obligations, and enforcement mechanisms, and each requires specific contractual provisions in vendor agreements. Where a vendor processes data subject to multiple regimes (which is increasingly common in Pinnacle\'s vendor portfolio), the DPA must address all applicable requirements, and the most restrictive standard generally governs.

Negotiators should be aware that many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted primarily with GDPR in mind and may fail to address HIPAA or CCPA/CPRA requirements. It is the negotiator\'s responsibility to identify these gaps and require the addition of all necessary provisions before execution.
**[2.1 HIPAA / HITECH]{.underline}**

All DPAs with Business Associates **MUST** incorporate a **Business Associate Agreement** (\"**BAA**\"), either as an integrated section within the DPA body or as a standalone exhibit appended to and expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. This requirement is non-negotiable and derives from the mandatory contractual provisions set forth in **45 CFR § 164.502(e)** and **45 CFR § 164.504(e)**.
A compliant BAA must include, at a minimum, the following elements:

7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));

8\. **Record retention of six (6) years** per 45 CFR § 164.530(j), covering all HIPAA-required documentation including the BAA itself, policies and procedures, training records, and incident records; and

9\. **Return or destruction of PHI at termination**, with exceptions where return or destruction is infeasible, in which case the protections of the BAA must extend to all retained PHI for as long as it is maintained.

Negotiators should be particularly alert to vendor DPA templates that reference GDPR Article 28 processor requirements but omit any reference to HIPAA. Where a vendor will process PHI, the absence of a BAA renders the DPA non-compliant regardless of how robust the GDPR provisions may be.
**[2.2 CCPA / CPRA]{.underline}**

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient-facing platform, provider network, and marketing and analytics activities. This volume substantially exceeds the CCPA/CPRA applicability thresholds and places Pinnacle squarely within the statute\'s scope as a \"**Business**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d).

Vendors that process California personal information on Pinnacle\'s behalf must qualify as \"**Service Providers**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag). The Service Provider designation is not automatic; it requires specific contractual provisions that restrict the vendor\'s use, retention, and disclosure of personal information received from Pinnacle. Without these contractual provisions, a vendor may be deemed a \"third party\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which could expose Pinnacle to claims that it has \"sold\" or \"shared\" personal information in violation of the statute.

> • A **prohibition on combining** personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information received from any other person or entity, or collected from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA;

These provisions are mandatory for all vendors with access to California resident data. A vendor DPA that omits these provisions, or that contains language inconsistent with the Service Provider classification, must be redlined before execution. Detailed negotiation positions for CCPA/CPRA terms are set forth in Section 7 of this playbook.
**[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**
Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
> • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;

GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.

**[3.1 Required Defined Terms by Regulatory Regime]{.underline}**

**[3.2 Negotiation Positions for Definitions]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA must include all three sets of definitions where the vendor processes data subject to multiple regulatory regimes. Many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted to address GDPR only and will include GDPR definitions but omit HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA definitions entirely. Where this is the case, the negotiator must require the addition of both the HIPAA definitions and the CCPA/CPRA definitions before the DPA is finalized. A DPA that covers PHI but lacks the defined term \"Protected Health Information\" creates ambiguity regarding the scope of the vendor\'s obligations and may be insufficient to satisfy the BAA requirements of 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Similarly, a DPA that covers California personal information but lacks the defined terms \"Service Provider,\" \"Sale,\" and \"Share\" may fail to establish the vendor\'s qualification as a Service Provider under the CCPA/CPRA, with potentially significant regulatory consequences for Pinnacle.

**Nice-to-have:** A single, integrated definitions section within the DPA body, rather than separate definitions scattered across the DPA, BAA exhibit, and CCPA addendum. An integrated definitions section reduces the risk of inconsistent or conflicting definitions and simplifies interpretation and enforcement.

**Fallback:** HIPAA definitions may be incorporated by reference to the BAA exhibit, and CCPA/CPRA definitions may be incorporated by reference to a CCPA/CPRA Addendum, so long as both the BAA exhibit and the CCPA/CPRA Addendum are appended to and expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should confirm that the cross-references are accurate and that the defined terms in the exhibit or addendum are consistent with the terms used in the DPA body.
**[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.

ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
**[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:

> **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.

> **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.
> \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.

> **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
> **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.

> **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.

> **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.

**Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.

**Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
**[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**

Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.

If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.

For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.

Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.

Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.

This telephonic-plus-written approach allows Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team to begin its assessment in parallel with the vendor\'s investigation.

The allocation of financial risk between Pinnacle and its vendors must reflect the magnitude of the data at stake, the severity of potential regulatory penalties, and the operational and reputational harm that a data breach or compliance failure could cause. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required liability framework, including liability caps, carve-outs, and indemnification obligations.

Pinnacle\'s position on liability is informed by the following considerations: (i) a breach of PHI affecting Pinnacle\'s approximately 2.1 million US patients could result in HIPAA penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year, plus class action litigation exposure; (ii) a CCPA/CPRA violation could result in statutory damages of \$100 to \$750 per consumer per incident, which at 890,000 California residents represents potential exposure of \$89 million to \$667.5 million; and (iii) GDPR penalties can reach up to €20 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Against this backdrop, vendor liability caps that are a fraction of annual fees are commercially unreasonable and legally inadequate.
**[6.1 Liability Cap]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** Vendor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under the DPA must be no less than **two times (2x) the total annual fees** attributable to the affected data processing activity.
**Must-have:** Liability must be **uncapped** for the following categories of claims:
> \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.

**Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.

**Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.

**Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.
**[6.2 Indemnification]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Vendor must indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Pinnacle, its officers, directors, employees, agents, and affiliates (including Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.) from and against all losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of litigation) arising from or related to:

> \(a\) **Third-party claims** (including claims by data subjects, consumers, patients, and healthcare providers) arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or any applicable data protection law;

> \(c\) **Costs of breach response**, including but not limited to: costs of breach notification to affected individuals and regulatory authorities; costs of credit monitoring and identity theft protection services provided to affected individuals; costs of forensic investigation; costs of public relations and crisis communications; and costs of regulatory reporting and compliance remediation, in each case to the extent arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or applicable data protection law.

Indemnification obligations should be subject to the same uncapped/capped structure as direct liability set forth in Section 6.1 above. Specifically, indemnification for claims arising from willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional breaches of confidentiality, and regulatory fines resulting from vendor non-compliance must be uncapped. Indemnification for all other claims may be subject to the aggregate liability cap (2x annual fees), but must not be subject to any lower cap or sublimit.
**[Section 7: CCPA / CPRA Service Provider Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section sets forth the mandatory contractual provisions that must appear in all DPAs where the vendor processes personal information of California residents on Pinnacle\'s behalf. These provisions are required to establish the vendor\'s status as a \"Service Provider\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which is essential to Pinnacle\'s compliance with the statute.
**[7.1 Service Provider Contractual Terms]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA must include the following CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag):

> **(b) Purpose Limitation.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle for any purpose other than performing the services specified in the DPA and the applicable MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement. Vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information for vendor\'s own business purposes, including but not limited to marketing, product development, analytics, or profiling, unless such use is expressly authorized by Pinnacle in writing and is consistent with a permissible business purpose under the CCPA/CPRA.

> **(d) Prohibition on Combining.** Vendor is prohibited from combining personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information that vendor receives from or on behalf of any other person or entity, or that vendor collects from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA (e.g., to detect data security incidents or protect against fraud).

> **(e) Service Provider Certification.** Vendor must include a certification, executed by an authorized representative of vendor, stating that vendor understands the restrictions set forth in subparagraphs (a) through (d) above and will comply with them. This certification is a statutory requirement under the CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and must appear in the DPA itself or in a CCPA/CPRA Addendum appended to the DPA.

> **(f) Right to Monitor Compliance.** Vendor must grant Pinnacle the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that vendor uses personal information in a manner consistent with Pinnacle\'s obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. This includes the right to conduct ongoing manual reviews, automated scans, and assessments of vendor\'s systems and practices as they relate to the processing of personal information received from Pinnacle.

> **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor agrees to cooperate with Pinnacle in responding to CCPA/CPRA consumer requests, including the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), and the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), within timelines consistent with the statute. Under the CCPA/CPRA, Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor\'s cooperation must be sufficiently prompt to allow Pinnacle to meet these deadlines.

**Fallback:** If the vendor\'s DPA template contains no CCPA/CPRA provisions whatsoever, Pinnacle will require a **standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum** appended to the DPA. The addendum must contain all of the provisions listed in subparagraphs (a) through (g) above and must be expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should use the template language provided in Appendix B as a starting point for drafting the addendum.
